title: Genes, adaptation and extinction

oak.unit: Adaptations, competition, natural selection and evolution, Year 9
Adaptations, competition, natural selection and evolution, Year 9

big_idea: Adaptations come from genes; when the environment changes, a species may no longer be well adapted and can become endangered or extinct, so we protect biodiversity.
goals: I can explain how changes in abiotic and biotic factors can make a species endangered or extinct, using the idea of adaptations.
I can describe ways of preserving biodiversity, including nature reserves, breeding programmes and gene banks.

keywords.meaning: a characteristic that helps an organism survive in its habitat
a species in danger of becoming extinct
a species with no living members left
a non-living part of the environment, e.g. rainfall, temperature
the activities of other organisms, e.g. competition, disease, hunting
when organisms need the same limited resource, e.g. food or light
a species that is naturally found in a part of the world
the number of different species in an area or on Earth
an area where habitats and species are protected
breeding endangered animals or plants in captivity to increase their numbers
a store of seeds, gametes or cells kept cold so a species can be grown again

misconceptions: Animals compete only by fighting. Most competition is for food, water, space, light or mates; the grey squirrel wins by eating acorns first, not by fighting.

Organisms choose to adapt when the environment changes. Adaptations are inherited characteristics from genes; an individual cannot change its genes, so a species that is no longer well adapted declines.
Conservation only happens in big wild places. Gene banks, zoos and small local reserves also preserve biodiversity.

slides.subtitle: How can genetic information cause extinction?
slides.notes: This lesson links adaptations (from genes) to environmental change. It prepares the ground for natural selection next lesson: here the question is why a species declines when it is no longer well adapted.

slides.title: Do Now: the day the dinosaurs died
slides.caption: Artist's impression of the impact
prompt: About 65 million years ago a giant meteorite hit the Earth near Mexico, throwing up so much dust that it blocked out sunlight. 75% of species became extinct.
1. State one physical environmental factor that the meteorite changed.
2. Explain the effect this had on plants.
3. Explain the effect this had on animals.
slides.notes: Light (and temperature) fell. Plants could not photosynthesise, so many died. Animals that ate plants starved, then the predators that ate them. Evidence: a 180 km wide crater near Mexico formed at this time.

slides.title: Today
slides.notes: Read the goals. Remind students that abiotic and biotic factors were Lesson 1's key words; today they are the causes of extinction.

slides.title: The last thylacine
slides.question: Thylacines were killed in Tasmania to protect sheep. The last one died in a zoo in 1936. Which environmental factor caused this extinction: abiotic or biotic?
slides.caption: A thylacine photographed in 1933
text: Talk to a partner: name two other human activities that can make a species extinct.
slides.notes: Biotic: hunting is an activity of other organisms (people). Other human activities: clearing habitats for farms and towns, using poisons, bringing in new species that compete or carry disease, fishing too much.

slides.title: Adaptations, genes and change
slides.caption: A sand cat's fur matches the sand it hunts on
text: The adaptations of an organism are due to its genes.
If the ecosystem changes, a species may no longer be well adapted to the new conditions.
Its numbers fall: it becomes endangered, and may become extinct.
Changes in abiotic factors: rainfall, temperature, light. Changes in biotic factors: competition, disease, human activities (hunting, clearing habitats, poisons).
slides.key_idea: A species cannot change its genes to fit a new environment; if it is no longer well adapted, it declines.
slides.notes: Sand cats are camouflaged against sand. Ask: if the desert got greener, would the camouflage still work? This links to the gap fill at Core. Stress that an individual cannot choose to change its adaptations.

slides.title: Grey squirrels and red squirrels
slides.caption: The grey squirrel was brought to the UK from the USA in the 1870s
text: Red squirrels are native to the UK. Greys were brought from the USA in the 1870s; now reds are rare.
Greys store more body fat, so more survive a long winter.
Greys can digest unripe acorns; reds cannot. Greys eat the acorns first, so reds get less food.
Greys carry squirrel pox, which does not harm greys but kills reds.
slides.key_idea: When food is limited, the better adapted competitor survives and reproduces more, and its population grows faster.
slides.notes: These are inherited differences between the two species: the greys' genes give them more fat storage and the ability to digest unripe acorns. Competition and disease are both biotic factors.

slides.title: Two squirrels, many shared adaptations

left.heading: Both species
points: Eyes on the side of the head: all-round vision to spot predators.
Long, strong hind legs for leaping.
Sharp claws for gripping tree trunks.

right.heading: Differences
points: Greys are bigger and store more fat: better in long winters.
Greys digest unripe acorns: eat them before the reds.
Greys carry squirrel pox, which kills reds.
Reds are lighter: better on thin, flexible conifer branches, and eat small conifer seeds.

slides.key_idea: Which species is 'better adapted' depends on the habitat: reds still do well in conifer forests.
slides.notes: Ask the Stretch question now: why might reds be better adapted to conifer forests than greys? Smaller, lighter animals can move on thin flexible branches and handle small seeds.

slides.title: Preserving biodiversity
slides.caption: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores seeds from around the world
text: Biodiversity is the number of different species.
Extinctions upset ecosystems and food webs, and we lose species we could use (food, medicines).
Ways to preserve biodiversity: ban hunting of certain animals, set up nature reserves, run breeding programmes.
Gene banks store seeds, gametes or cells at low temperatures, so a species can be produced again if it becomes extinct in the wild.
slides.key_idea: Protect the habitat, protect the animals, and keep a frozen back-up of the genes.
slides.notes: The Svalbard vault in the Arctic holds over a million seed samples. Ask: why keep seeds cold? (They stay alive for decades without growing.) Why is a gene bank not enough on its own? (A species also needs a habitat to live in.)

slides.title: Quick check
questions: Give one adaptation that red and grey squirrels share.
Why do grey squirrels get more acorns than reds?
Give one way of preserving biodiversity.
slides.notes: Answers: in danger of becoming extinct; biotic; e.g. bushy tail for balance; they can digest unripe acorns so they eat them first; nature reserves, breeding programmes, hunting bans, gene banks.

slides.title: Your turn: adaptation and extinction
steps: Core: match the environment words; sand cat gap fill; native species and competition; resources plants compete for.
Stretch: explain the squirrel story with adaptations and genes; reds in conifer forests; the sundew and rising temperature.
Challenge: Haast's eagle and the moa; how a gene bank works and what it cannot do.
Use 'better adapted' and 'genes' in every explanation.
slides.footer: A good explanation says what changed, why the species was no longer well adapted, and what happened to its numbers.
slides.notes: The sundew question (Stretch 3): warmer temperature means more evaporation, the bog dries, and a plant with tiny roots cannot get enough water. The Haast's eagle question is about losing its prey (a biotic factor).

slides.title: Polar bears and a warming world
slides.prompt: Polar bears hunt seals from the sea ice. Global warming is making the Arctic sea ice melt earlier each year. Predict the effect on the polar bear population and explain your reasoning.
slides.caption: A polar bear on sea ice
frames: I predict the population will ___ because ___.
The abiotic factor that is changing is ___.
Polar bears are adapted to ___, so when ___ they cannot ___.
slides.notes: Expected: the population falls because less sea ice means less time to hunt seals, so bears starve and have fewer cubs; the abiotic factor is temperature (and ice cover). Their adaptations (white fur, fat layer, hunting on ice) do not help when the ice is gone.

slides.title: Exit ticket
questions: What does it mean if a species is endangered?
Give one biotic factor that can cause a species to become extinct.
Give one way of preserving biodiversity and say how it works.
slides.notes: Answers: in danger of becoming extinct; e.g. competition from a new species, disease, hunting, habitat clearing; e.g. a gene bank stores seeds or gametes cold so the species can be grown again; a nature reserve protects the habitat; a breeding programme increases numbers in captivity.

slides.title: What we learned
slides.next: Natural selection and evolution: how the environment 'selects' the inherited variations that survive, and how new species form.
points: Adaptations come from genes. When abiotic or biotic factors change, a species may no longer be well adapted and can become endangered or extinct.
Competition, disease and human activities are biotic factors that can cause extinction; the grey squirrel out-competes the red.
Biodiversity is the number of different species; losing species damages ecosystems and food webs.
We preserve biodiversity with hunting bans, nature reserves, breeding programmes and gene banks.

worksheet.my_thinking: Red squirrels died out in some parts of the UK in the 1980s and there are plans to reintroduce them. What could be done to help the reintroduced red squirrels survive?
exit: What does it mean if a species is endangered?

core: environment: an organism's surroundings; environmental factor: a part of the surroundings that can change an organism; abiotic factor: a non-living (physical) part of the surroundings; biotic factor: the activities of other organisms; environmental variation: differences caused by the surroundings.
adaptations; habitats; inherited; desert; camouflaged; camouflaged; endangered.
Any three of: light, water, space, mineral salts (nutrients), carbon dioxide.
stretch: a) Less food is available (fewer nuts and seeds), so squirrels without enough stored fat starve, and cold increases the energy they need. b) Greys store more fat in their bodies, so they can survive longer without food; they can also digest unripe acorns, so they get food before the reds. c) Secure answer: the amount of fat stored and the ability to digest unripe acorns are inherited characteristics controlled by the greys' genes; reds do not have these genes, so they cannot develop the same adaptations.

Reds are smaller and lighter, so they can move along thin, flexible branches that would not hold the heavier greys, and their smaller size suits eating many small conifer seeds; greys need bigger food such as acorns.

Secure answer: higher temperatures increase evaporation, so the bog becomes drier; sundews have very small roots adapted to wet conditions, so they cannot reach or absorb enough water from drier soil and may die, and other plants adapted to drier conditions may out-compete them.
challenge: a) e.g. very large size and powerful talons to kill a large bird; strong wings for carrying heavy prey; sharp eyesight to spot moa from above. b) The moa were the eagles' main food (a biotic factor). When humans hunted the moa to extinction, the eagles lost their prey; their adaptations suited hunting large flightless birds and there were no other prey of that size, so the eagles starved and could not raise young, and the species became extinct.

Seeds (or cells) are collected and stored at low temperature, where they stay alive for many years without growing; if the species dies out in the wild, the seeds can be germinated and the plants grown and planted out again. Limitation: the plants still need a suitable habitat to survive in; if the habitat has been destroyed or the climate has changed, they cannot be reintroduced; also a seed bank holds only a sample of the species' genetic variation.
exit: e.g. competition from an introduced species, a new disease, hunting, clearing of habitats.

e.g. a nature reserve protects the habitat so the species has somewhere to live; a breeding programme raises numbers in captivity and releases animals; a gene bank stores seeds or gametes cold to regrow the species.
answers.my_thinking: e.g. choose conifer forest areas where reds are better adapted; remove or control grey squirrels nearby; vaccinate or keep greys with squirrel pox away; provide extra food in winter; protect the habitat as a nature reserve; monitor the population.
